stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Urban trees are often treated as decoration, but they also perform practical environmental work. Their crowns shade streets and buildings, reducing the amount of heat absorbed by pavement and walls during the day. Leaves release water vapour, a process called transpiration, which can cool nearby air. Together, these effects may make tree-lined areas more comfortable during hot weather.
The benefits are not distributed automatically. A young tree provides little shade, and trees need sufficient water and suitable soil to grow. In crowded streets, roots may have limited space, while nearby construction can damage them. City planners therefore need to select species suited to local conditions and provide care during the years before trees mature.
Trees can also improve everyday urban life in less direct ways. A shaded footpath may encourage walking, and a green public space can offer residents a place to pause. Yet planting trees is not a complete solution to rising temperatures: buildings, transport, and energy use also affect urban heat. The most useful approach is to combine well-planned greenery with measures that reduce heat at its sources. In this way, trees are neither mere ornaments nor a substitute for broader planning, but a practical part of it.

What is the passage mainly about?
options: Urban trees provide practical benefits, but they require planning and complement other measures.
Urban trees are mainly decorative features that make streets more attractive to residents.
Planting trees is the most effective way to solve rising temperatures in cities.
Urban trees are useful only when they cool streets during hot weather.
